\chapter{Introduction}
Irrigation districts in the Marmara basin face a tightening gap
between contracted water rights and reliable supply.
Surface deliveries from the cascade reservoirs have declined
in four of the last six years,
while aquifer levels in the coastal plain continue to fall.

Conjunctive use --- the coordinated drawing on surface and groundwater ---
is the standard policy answer,
yet the district-level rules that would implement it remain informal.
Farmers report ad hoc rotations negotiated each spring,
and the basin authority lacks a transparent allocation formula.

This report assembles the delivery, pumping, and cropping records
for the 2019--2025 period,
estimates the shadow value of water under the current rules,
and evaluates two candidate allocation formulas
against the status quo.

\chapter{Institutional Background}
Water rights in the basin are held by irrigation cooperatives
and administered through annual delivery schedules.
The schedules are nominally proportional to contracted area,
but late-season reductions are allocated by seniority,
which shifts drought risk onto junior districts.

Groundwater use is licensed but weakly metered.
Well permits specify an annual volume,
yet enforcement relies on self-reporting,
and pumping is widely believed to exceed licensed amounts
in dry years.

Earlier studies of the basin have treated surface and groundwater
as separate sectors.
The few joint analyses predate the 2021 reallocation
of reservoir capacity to municipal supply.

\chapter{Data}
The analysis combines three administrative sources:
delivery records from the basin authority,
cooperative pumping logs,
and the annual cropping census.
All series cover the eleven districts for 2019--2025.

Delivered volumes are recorded weekly at each turnout.
Pumping logs are monthly and are adjusted for the meter
coverage rate in each district.
Cropping patterns are observed at the parcel level
and aggregated to the district.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Variable & Mean & Std.\ dev. \\
\midrule
Surface delivery (dam$^3$/ha) & 4.6 & 1.3 \\
Pumping (dam$^3$/ha) & 2.9 & 1.7 \\
Cereals share (\%) & 58 & 12 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{District-year summary statistics, 2019--2025.}
\end{table}

A regression of delivered volume on contracted area and
district fixed effects yields $R^2^{adj} = 0.81$,
indicating that the schedule explains most of the
cross-district variation in normal years.

\chapter{Methods}
We estimate the shadow value of water with a restricted
profit function.
For district $i$ in year $t$, observed profit is modelled as
\begin{equation}
\pi_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 s_{it} + \beta_2 g_{it}
+ \beta_3 s_{it} g_{it} + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it},
\end{equation}
where $s_{it}$ and $g_{it}$ are surface and groundwater
volumes per hectare and $\lambda_t$ is a year effect.

The interaction term captures substitutability between
the two sources.
Under the null of perfect substitutability, $\beta_3 = 0$;
a negative estimate indicates that conjunctive use
generates scarcity rents.

Standard errors are clustered at the district level.
Instruments for pumping are constructed from
electricity tariffs and aquifer depth.

\chapter{Results}
The estimated shadow price of surface water averages
1.9 lira per cubic metre over the sample period.
In drought years the price roughly doubles,
and the premium for senior districts widens.

For the median district, a one dam$^3$ reduction in
surface delivery lowers pumping costs net of yield losses
by $\gama = 0.13$ lira per cubic metre,
so groundwater buffers about a third of the surface shortfall.
The interaction term is negative and significant,
rejecting perfect substitutability.

Both candidate allocation formulas raise basin-wide profit
relative to the status quo,
with the larger gains under the proportional-deficit rule.

\chapter{Conclusion}
Conjunctive use in the Marmara basin already buffers
a substantial share of surface scarcity,
but the gains are captured unevenly across districts.
A transparent proportional-deficit rule would redistribute
drought risk without reducing basin-wide profit.

The main limitation of this report is the reliance on
self-reported pumping.
A metering pilot in two districts is scheduled for 2027
and should permit a sharper welfare analysis.
